title: NABL for Medical Laboratories
shortDescription: The most exam-relevant chapter for microbiology and clinical-lab students — the pre-examination, examination, and post-examination process, and everything a medical lab must control to earn and keep accreditation.
genZNote: This is the chapter where ‘accreditation’ stops being an abstract word and becomes your actual daily bench routine.

sections.heading: What Is a Medical Laboratory, and Why Does Accreditation Matter?
sections.body:
A medical laboratory examines materials derived from the human body — blood, urine, tissue, swabs — to provide information for diagnosis, monitoring, treatment, and prevention of disease. Because clinical decisions are made directly on a lab's results, an error here has a direct patient-safety consequence, not just a quality-metric one.

Accreditation to ISO 15189 gives an independent, ongoing check that a lab's people, equipment, methods, and processes are competent — not a one-time inspection, but a maintained state.

sections.heading: The Three-Phase Examination Process
sections.body: ISO 15189 and NABL both structure a medical lab's work into three phases. Nearly every quality-control concept in this chapter attaches to one of these three.

steps.name: Pre-examination
steps.explanation: Everything before the sample is actually tested: patient/sample identification, correct sample collection, proper transport and storage, and request handling.
steps.purpose: Most laboratory errors worldwide happen here, not during testing itself — a mislabelled sample can never be fixed by a perfect test.

steps.name: Examination
steps.explanation: The actual testing: applying validated/verified methods, running internal quality control alongside patient samples, using calibrated equipment and controlled reagents.
steps.purpose: This is where analytical accuracy and precision are actually produced.

steps.name: Post-examination
steps.explanation: Result validation, interpretation, timely reporting, flagging and communicating critical results, and appropriate storage/retention of samples and records.
steps.purpose: A correct result that's reported late, to the wrong person, or without a critical-value alert can still harm the patient.

sections.heading: Quality Control & Quality Assurance on the Bench
bullets: Internal quality control (IQC) — running known control materials alongside patient samples, every run, to catch drift before it reaches a patient result.
External quality assessment (EQA) / proficiency testing (PT) — periodically testing a sample of unknown value sent by an outside provider, to compare your lab's result against peer labs.
Equipment management — calibration, maintenance, and performance verification on a defined schedule, with records.
Reagent management — correct storage, lot tracking, and expiry control.
Method verification/validation — confirming a method performs as claimed (verification) or establishing its performance from scratch (validation) before it's used on patients.
Personnel competence — documented training, assessment, and periodic re-assessment of every person performing or authorising a result.
Traceability and measurement uncertainty — results traceable to recognised reference standards where applicable, with a documented understanding of how much uncertainty a measurement carries.

sections.heading: Nonconforming Work, Corrective Action, and Risk
sections.body: When something doesn't meet requirements — a failed control, a complaint, an equipment fault — it's nonconforming work. The lab must contain it (stop it reaching a patient report), investigate the root cause, take corrective action so it doesn't recur, and verify that the action actually worked. Risk management sits alongside this proactively: identifying what COULD go wrong in a process before it does, and controlling it in advance rather than only reacting after an error.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: NABL accredits medical laboratories against ISO 15189, assessing competence across the pre-examination, examination, and post-examination phases of patient testing.
keyFacts: IQC checks precision/accuracy during routine testing; EQA/PT compares a lab's performance against outside peer labs.
Most pre-analytical errors occur before the sample is ever tested — identification and collection are critical control points.
Method verification confirms an existing method works as claimed; method validation establishes a new/modified method's performance from scratch.
Nonconforming work must be contained, investigated, corrected, and the correction's effectiveness verified.
commonConfusion: IQC checks the lab's OWN ongoing performance run-to-run. EQA/PT checks the lab's performance AGAINST other labs, using an outside provider's samples — they are complementary, not substitutes for each other.

highYieldFacts: The three-phase process (pre-examination → examination → post-examination) is the backbone of ISO 15189 and NABL medical-lab assessment.
IQC is internal and continuous; EQA/PT is external and periodic.
Critical result reporting is a post-examination requirement with direct patient-safety weight.
commonTraps: Assuming quality control only applies during testing — pre- and post-examination steps are assessed just as heavily.
Confusing method verification (confirming an existing method) with method validation (establishing a new one).
mustRemember: Sample identification and collection errors (pre-examination) are the single most common source of lab error.
IQC = internal, ongoing. EQA/PT = external, periodic, peer-compared.

confusedTerms.distinction: IQC uses the lab's own control materials, run alongside patient samples, to monitor day-to-day precision. EQA/PT uses samples from an outside provider to compare the lab's results against other participating laboratories.

possibleQuestions: Explain the three-phase examination process with one quality risk from each phase.
A medical laboratory wants to demonstrate competence in its examination processes end-to-end. Which accreditation framework is most directly relevant, and why?

sources.name: NABL — National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories

pathways.title: The Examination Process, Start to Finish
steps: Request received — correct patient and test identified
Sample collected, labelled, and transported under proper conditions (Pre-examination)
Sample tested with validated methods, IQC run alongside (Examination)
Result reviewed, validated, and critical values flagged (Post-examination)
Report issued to the requesting clinician, with records retained

questions.prompt: A mislabelled blood sample reaches the lab. Which phase of the examination process does this error belong to?
options: None — labelling is outside the examination process
questions.explanation: Sample identification and collection are pre-examination activities — and the single most common source of laboratory error.

questions.prompt: Running a known control sample alongside every batch of patient samples is an example of:
questions.explanation: This is IQC — an internal, ongoing check run by the lab itself.

questions.prompt: True or False: Method verification and method validation mean exactly the same thing.
questions.explanation: Verification confirms an already-established method performs as claimed in your lab; validation establishes the performance of a new or modified method from scratch.
